passages.text: In the early phase of thinking about advanced technologies, nanotechnology was seen as one of the most powerful scientific developments. It refers to the manipulation of matter at an extremely small scale, such as atoms and molecules. During the early 2000s, some scientists and engineers proposed very ambitious ideas about what nanotechnology could achieve in the future. One of the most famous contributors to this vision was K. Eric Drexler, who suggested that tiny machines, called nanobots, could one day build almost anything by arranging atoms one by one. These ideas created huge excitement because they seemed to offer solutions to many human problems. Nanobots were imagined as machines that could cure diseases, remove poverty, and even extend human life significantly. Some extreme versions of this vision also suggested that humans could transfer their minds into machines and achieve a form of digital immortality. Along with this optimism, there were also serious fears. One major concern was the idea of "grey goo," a scenario in which self-replicating nanobots could multiply uncontrollably and consume all matter on Earth. However, as scientific understanding improved, these ideas came under strong criticism. Researchers pointed out that such visions were not supported by real scientific evidence. At the molecular level, matter does not behave like mechanical systems such as gears or machines. Instead, it is governed by complex chemical interactions and random motion, which makes precise control at that level extremely difficult. In reality, nanotechnology has developed in a much more limited and practical direction. Instead of building tiny robots, scientists have focused on using chemistry and materials science to create useful applications. These include developments in medicine, electronics, and imaging technologies. While these advancements are important, they are far less dramatic than the original futuristic predictions. Many technological visions are shaped more by imagination than by actual scientific possibility. These ideas often promise perfect futures without suffering, death, or limitations, which makes them attractive but unrealistic. Such exaggerated predictions can sometimes distract attention from real scientific progress that solves practical problems. Today, similar patterns can be seen in discussions about other emerging technologies as well. Bold claims and fears often develop faster than actual scientific progress. Therefore, it becomes important to carefully evaluate such ideas and separate realistic science from speculative imagination. (360 words, by No suffering, no death, no limits: the nanobots pipe dream)

passages.text: Niccolao Manucci was a Venetian traveller who came to India in the 17th century and spent most of his life there. He is known for writing one of the earliest European accounts of the Mughal Empire called Storia do Mogor. His work is considered valuable because it provides detailed descriptions of Mughal rulers, court life, and everyday customs in India during that period. Manucci travelled across many regions of India, worked under different rulers, and also served in roles such as soldier, physician, and interpreter. Manucci's travel account is important for historians because it gives first-hand observations of political events and social life in Mughal India. He wrote about major figures like Aurangzeb, Shah Jahan, and Dara Shikoh. However, his writings are not always fully reliable. Scholars have pointed out that his memoir contains both factual information and exaggerated or inaccurate details. This makes it necessary for historians to carefully verify his claims using other sources. Despite these limitations, Manucci's work remains significant because very few Europeans lived in India for such a long period during that time. He observed not only royal courts but also local customs, traditions, and everyday life of people. His writings include descriptions of food habits, social practices, and cultural differences between Europeans and Indians. These details help modern researchers understand historical India beyond just political history. Manucci's life in India was full of movement and change. He worked with different rulers and communities, which allowed him to experience diverse regions and cultures. Eventually, he settled in southern India, where he continued writing his memoirs. His travelogue was later published in Europe and became an important historical source for studying the Mughal period. Overall, Manucci's account is both valuable and complex. While it provides rare historical insight, it must be read critically due to its mix of accurate observation and personal interpretation. (300 words, by The Indian travelogue of Niccolao Manucci)

passages.text: There was no hope for him this time: it was the third stroke. Night after night I had passed the house (it was vacation time) and studied the lighted square of window: and night after night I had found it lighted in the same way, faintly and evenly. If he was dead, I thought, I would see the reflection of candles on the darkened blind for I knew that two candles must be set at the head of a corpse. He had often said to me: "I am not long for this world," and I had thought his words idle. Now I knew they were true. Every night as I gazed up at the window I said softly to myself the word paralysis. It had always sounded strangely in my ears, like the word gnomon in the Euclid and the word simony in the Catechism. But now it sounded to me like the name of some maleficent and sinful being. It filled me with fear, and yet I longed to be nearer to it and to look upon its deadly work. Old Cotter was sitting at the fire, smoking, when I came downstairs to supper. While my aunt was ladling out my stirabout he said, as if returning to some former remark of his: "No, I wouldn't say he was exactly ... but there was something queer ... there was something uncanny about him. I'll tell you my opinion...." He began to puff at his pipe, no doubt arranging his opinion in his mind. Tiresome old fool! When we knew him first he used to be rather interesting, talking of faints and worms; but I soon grew tired of him and his endless stories about the distillery. "I have my own theory about it," he said. "I think it was one of those ... peculiar cases.... But it's hard to say...." He began to puff again at his pipe without giving us his theory. My uncle saw me staring and said to me: "Well, so your old friend is gone, you'll be sorry to hear." "Who?" said I. "Father Flynn." "Is he dead?" "Mr Cotter here has just told us. He was passing by the house." I knew that I was under observation so I continued eating as if the news had not interested me. My uncle explained to old Cotter. "The youngster and he were great friends. The old chap taught him a great deal, mind you; and they say he had a great wish for him." "God have mercy on his soul," said my aunt piously. Old Cotter looked at me for a while. I felt that his little beady black eyes were examining me but I would not satisfy him by looking up from my plate. He returned to his pipe and finally spat rudely into the grate. (450 words, The Dubliners by James Joyce)

passages.text: Looking back, we will remember 2025 as the year of the great capitulation. It was the year liberal democracy lost its nerve, as law firms, universities, media organizations, corporations and countries appeased an increasingly illiberal United States in an unseemly and miscalculated scramble to get the best possible deals for themselves. Paradoxically, only China — hardly an avatar of liberal democracy — had the political will and the economic leverage to stand up to an American administration bent on rewriting the rules of the liberal international order that the United States itself had created. Beijing, it turned out, understood Washington better than many of America's allies did: appeasing a predatory hegemon doesn't work. What does work — as I learned when I led Canada's first renegotiation of NAFTA as the minister of foreign affairs in 2018 — is using the bargaining chips you have, including retaliating when you are attacked. In 2026 we should all learn that lesson. This should be the year that liberal democracy fights back, in earnest.In many ways, that fight is already underway. It began in countries like my own and Australia, where what had seemed like likely election victories for the populist right were stymied by a surge of patriotic resistance. A few months later, Norway and the Netherlands followed suit. (213 words, Editorial, The New York Times)

passages.text: An elated NASA on April 10, 2026 was celebrating its successful voyage around the Moon, after four astronauts safely returned to Earth having completed the first lunar flyby in more than 50 years. The NASA spacecraft carrying four astronauts - three Americans and one Canadian - splashed down without a hitch off the California coast, capping the US space agency's crewed test mission that returned with spectacular images of the Moon. From liftoff to splashdown, the trip clocked in at nine days, one hour, 31 minutes and 35 seconds - though NASA rounds up and calls it a 10-day mission. It began with a dramatic launch from Florida on April 1, and was studded with firsts, records and extraordinary moments. The four astronauts become the humans to travel furthest away from the Earth, at 252,756 miles (406,771 kilometers). While hurtling through deep space and zipping around the Moon they took thousands of photographs, amassing a stunning portfolio of images that captivated people on Earth. They also witnessed a solar eclipse along with extraordinary meteorite strikes on the lunar surface. Several achievements added to the voyage's historic nature: Mr. Glover was the first person of color to fly around the Moon, Ms. Koch was the first woman, and Canadian Hansen the first non-American. NASA is hoping it can put boots on the lunar surface as soon as 2028 -- the final full year of Trump's second White House term. Experts, however, have voiced skepticism that the lunar landers being developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin, companies owned by billionaires Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos respectively, will be ready in time. China, meanwhile, is forging ahead with its own effort targeting 2030 to put astronauts on the Moon. In the meantime, NASA is hoping to capitalize on the Artemis II mission's success to drum up excitement about space exploration. Clayton Swope, a space policy expert at of the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told AFP that the mission stands as "proof that when America keeps its eye on the prize, it can still do very great things."

passages.text: The Census 2027, world's largest census exercise has begun. The Government of India has commenced Phase I of Census 2027 - Houselisting and Housing Census (HLO) from today, marking the beginning of the country's largest administrative and statistical exercise. This is India's first ever digital data capture and Self-Enumeration. The national enumeration exercise was initiated with the enumeration of the President of India, Smt Droupadi Murmu, through the option of Self-Enumeration, upholding the proud tradition of commencing the national count with the First Citizen of India. The Vice-President, Shri C.P. Radhakrishnan filled out the self-enumeration form online for Census 2027, at Uprashtrapati Bhavan. The Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi completed his self-enumeration. Prime Minister appealed to the people of India to self-enumerate their household details themselves and participate in the Census process. In the first phase of rollout, Self-Enumeration process has commenced in eight States and Union Territories including Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Goa, Karnataka, Lakshadweep, Mizoram, Odisha, Sikkim, New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) area and Delhi Cantonment Board of the National Capital from 1st April 2026. About 55,000 households from these States/UTs availed Self-Enumeration facility on the very first day.The Houselisting and Housing Census in these States/UTs will begin from April 16, 2026 and will continue till May 15, 2026. The Self-Enumeration exercise is a secure, web-based facility available in 16 regional languages. For the first time, respondents can fill in their details online at their convenience before the enumerator's visit. Enumerators will carry out door-to-door visits in all allocated houselisitng blocks as in previous Censuses, while Self-Enumeration serves as an additional facility. To participate in Self- Enumeration, respondents can log in to the portal se.census.gov.in using their mobile number and basic credentials. Upon successful submission, a unique Self-Enumeration ID (SE ID) is generated, which will be shared with the enumerator during the subsequent field visit for confirmation. During the Houselisting and Housing Census phase, comprehensive information on the condition of housing, household amenities and assets possessed will be collected. A total of 33 questions for Phase I have been notified in January 2026 to capture these critical indicators, which serve as the foundation for evidence-based planning, policy formulation, and targeted welfare interventions.

passages.text: Shaheed Diwas, or Martyrs' Day, is a tribute to the bravery and devotion of India's freedom fighters who laid down their lives for the nation's independence. On March 23, 1931 - three revolutionary freedom fighters, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru, all in their early twenties, were hanged in the Lahore jail. The three were sentenced to death by the British colonial rulers. In 1928, the Simon Commission, an all- British panel, arrived in India to decide on its governance, sparking widespread protests. Lala Lajpat Rai, a prominent Indian freedom fighter, led a protest in Lahore on October 30, 1928. Police Superintendent James A. Scott ordered a baton charge, severely injuring Rai, who died of injuries from a police lathi charge on November 17, 1928. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru joined the freedom struggle and wanted to avenge the death of Lala Lajpat Rai. Their target was Superintendent of Police James Scott, who ordered the lathi charge, but in a case of mistaken identity, they ended up killing British police officer John Saunders instead. The three revolutionaries were part of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) and were influenced by socialist ideals. They were arrested, tried, and eventually sentenced to death for Saunders' murder. Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev were hanged on March 23, 1931, at Lahore Central Jail. Their execution sparked widespread outrage and protests, with many viewing them as martyrs who fought against British colonial rule. Today, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, and Rajguru are remembered as heroes of India's freedom struggle, and their legacy continues to inspire people across the country.

passages.text: The emergence of generative AI has posed significant doctrinal and ethical challenges to copyright law, particularly in jurisdictions governed by statutes such as the Copyright Act, 1957. Copyright protects "original works of authorship," requiring a minimal degree of creativity and, traditionally, human authorship. However, AI systems are trained on massive datasets, often scraped from the internet, which may include copyrighted works used without express authorization. A central legal issue is whether such use constitutes infringement or falls within exceptions like "fair dealing" under Section 52 of the Act. Courts have historically interpreted fair dealing narrowly, focusing on purpose, character, and market impact. While AI developers argue that training is "transformative," critics assert that large-scale, non-consensual ingestion of copyrighted material may substitute the original market or unjustly exploit creators' economic rights. Authorship presents another doctrinal challenge. Copyright law presumes a human author; hence, fully autonomous AI-generated works may fail to qualify for protection. However, where a human exercises creative control through detailed prompts, selection, arrangement, or substantial editing, the output may satisfy the originality threshold. Ethically, concerns arise regarding transparency, attribution, and bias. The opaque nature of AI training complicates identifying whose works were used and whether consent or compensation was provided. Scholars argue for a regulatory framework that ensures accountability while fostering innovation. Thus, the evolving legal landscape must reconcile statutory principles with technological realities, balancing the protection of creators with the advancement of AI.

passages.text: Section 26 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 renders void every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor. The provision is founded on public policy that treats the freedom to marry as an essential personal liberty. Courts have consistently interpreted this rule strictly: both absolute and partial restraints-whether based on time, person, class, or circumstance-are void if they substantially interfere with the choice to marry. However, the application of this principle often turns on whether a condition constitutes a real restraint or merely an incidental or regulatory provision. Courts have, in certain cases, upheld conditions that affect property or conduct, provided they do not operate as a direct prohibition or deterrent against marriage. The distinction is subtle: a condition that merely postpones enjoyment of a benefit without penalizing marriage may be treated differently from one that withdraws or forfeits a benefit upon marriage. Further complexity arises in the context of minors. Section 26 expressly excludes minors, not to validate restraints on their marriage, but because minors lack contractual capacity. Issues concerning child marriage are governed instead by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, under which a child marriage is generally voidable at the option of the minor, except in specified aggravated circumstances where it is void ab initio. Thus, while contract law does not directly invalidate restraints concerning minors, it does not endorse them either. The interplay of these principles requires careful evaluation of the substance, effect, and surrounding context of each condition. The law does not merely look at the form of the agreement but examines whether the condition, in practical terms, discourages or restricts marriage.

passages.text: The modern law of the sea is primarily governed by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which establishes a comprehensive framework regulating maritime zones, state rights, and navigation freedoms. Coastal states exercise varying degrees of control over different maritime zones measured from their baseline, typically the low-water line along the coast. Within territorial waters, extending up to 12 nautical miles, the coastal state enjoys full sovereignty, subject only to the right of "innocent passage" granted to foreign vessels. Passage is considered innocent so long as it is not prejudicial to the peace, good order, or security of the coastal state. Activities such as weapons exercises, spying, or fishing may render passage non-innocent. Beyond this lies the contiguous zone, extending up to 24 nautical miles, where the coastal state may enforce laws relating to customs, taxation, immigration, and sanitation.Further outward is the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), extending up to 200 nautical miles, where the coastal state has sovereign rights for the purpose of exploring, exploiting, conserving, and managing natural resources. However, other states retain freedoms of navigation and overflight in the EEZ. The high seas, lying beyond national jurisdiction, are governed by the principle of freedom of the seas. No state may validly claim sovereignty over any part of the high seas, and all states enjoy freedoms including navigation, fishing, and scientific research, subject to certain international obligations. Conflicts often arise when states attempt to extend control beyond permissible limits or when the nature of an activity such as surveillance or resource extraction blurs the distinction between lawful use and violation of coastal state rights. The resolution of such disputes depends on interpreting the balance between sovereignty and shared global commons.

passages.text: The right to freedom of religion in India is constitutionally guaranteed under Article 25 of the Constitution of India and Article 26 of the Constitution of India. While both provisions protect religious liberty, they operate in distinct yet overlapping spheres. Article 25 guarantees to all persons the freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion. However, this right is not absolute and is expressly subject to public order, morality, health, and other provisions of Part III. Additionally, the State is empowered to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political, or other secular activity associated with religious practice. Article 26, on the other hand, confers rights specifically upon religious denominations or sections thereof. These include the right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, manage their own affairs in matters of religion, own and acquire property, and administer such property in accordance with law. Like Article 25, these rights are also subject to public order, morality, and health. A crucial doctrinal development in this context is the distinction between essential religious practices and secular or non-essential activities. Courts have consistently held that only those practices which are essential and integral to a religion are protected from State interference. Conversely, activities that are merely associated with religion but are secular in nature such as administration of property or financial management may be regulated by the State. Tensions often arise where the State seeks to intervene in religious institutions on grounds of reform, equality, or public welfare. For instance, legislation aimed at ensuring social reform or opening religious institutions to all sections of society may conflict with denominational autonomy. In such cases, courts undertake a balancing exercise between individual rights under Article 25, group rights under Article 26, and broader constitutional values such as equality and social justice.

passages.text: The guarantee of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India constitutes a foundational pillar of constitutional democracy, enabling the circulation of ideas, dissent, and critique. However, this guarantee is carefully structured rather than absolute. Under Article 19(2) of the Constitution of India, the State may impose reasonable restrictions on this freedom in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, and incitement to an offence. Judicial interpretation has consistently emphasized that restrictions must satisfy a test of reasonableness and proportionality, requiring a proximate nexus between the expression and the harm sought to be prevented. For instance, restrictions based on public order must demonstrate a direct and imminent threat rather than speculative or remote consequences. Similarly, the ground of security of the State is invoked only in cases involving serious threats such as rebellion or insurrection, and not mere criticism of government policies. The limitation based on decency or morality, particularly in cases of obscenity, has evolved over time. Courts assess whether the expression, taken as a whole, tends to deprave or corrupt, while also considering artistic, literary, or social value. The mere presence of explicit content does not automatically justify restriction if the larger message is socially relevant. The ground of defamation protects individual reputation against false and harmful statements, while contempt of court seeks to preserve the authority and integrity of the judiciary by restricting publications that may scandalize or prejudice judicial proceedings. Further, restrictions based on incitement to an offence require a close connection between the speech and the likelihood of unlawful action.

passages.text: The first set of talks in Islamabad provided a sense of Iran's internal tensions. Iranian delegations dispatched for talks with America are usually lean, disciplined and tightly briefed. The Islamabad one was anything but: it was composed of some 80 Iranians. They ranged from a seasoned diplomat who helped fine-tune a nuclear deal with the Obama administration in 2015, to a firebrand who derides America as "a vicious yellow dog" and sneers that any deal would be capitulation. Their arguments were so ferocious that Pakistani mediators are reported to have spent as much time refereeing among the Iranians as engaging the Americans. One cause of the tensions is the existence of a vacuum at the top. Seven weeks after an American-Israeli air strike killed Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader for 37 years, his successors have failed to find a date for his funeral. His son and designated successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, is thought to be either incapacitated or too weak to impose authority. Since a ceasefire was declared on April 8th, the regime's wartime cohesion has begun to fray. Formally, authority rests with the Supreme National Security Council. Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker, has been designated as chief negotiator, with Mr Araghchi as his lieutenant. But their readiness to negotiate has provoked a backlash, particularly from the IRGC, the 190,000-strong force that defends the Islamic Republic. Inside Iran, signs of swelling military assertiveness are plentiful. Pro-regime crowds have taken to denouncing Mr Araghchi and Mr Ghalibaf by name. Military communiqués delivered by men in fatigues appear to have replaced clerical sermons. Some argue that the cacophony is tactical-a way to extract concessions by projecting hardline opposition. Yet the war appears to be hardening a new faultline between nationalists who are guided by realpolitik and state interest, and Islamists who are anchored in revolutionary ideology. Material interests muddy matters further. Over the years a class of generals-turned-sanction-busters has emerged: its members are thought to benefit handsomely from operations to circumvent American sanctions on the economy. With Khamenei senior gone, previously sidelined figures have re-emerged. Each group has a different view on the most important sticking-points in the talks, including the nuclear programme, control of Gulf waters and the role of Iran's regional proxies. Nationalists would trade proxy networks for sanctions relief; Islamists see them as the spine of "resistance". Even if Iran returns to talks, the deep divisions within the Iranian delegation mean both that it will be hard to reach a deal, and that any agreement with America could quickly unravel.

passages.text: The special session of Parliament to consider the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 - and also the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, and the Delimitation Bill, 2026 - for readjustment of Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly seats across the country and implementation of reservation of seats for women ended in a spectacular way. The proposed delimitation was to reallocate the number of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly seats among States, and determine the territorial boundaries of each constituency, based on data from the 2011 Census. The total number of Lok Sabha seats was proposed to be increased to 850. The special session was convened at a time when electioneering for the ongoing Legislative Assembly elections is at its peak in West Bengal and Tamil Nadu. Articles 82 and 170 (3) of the Constitution require a readjustment of the number of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats in each State and the extent of every constituency, after each Census. The first delimitation exercise in independent India was carried out in 1950-51 by the Election Commission of India. After the completion of the first general election, a fresh delimitation did take place based on the 1951 Census. Subsequently, readjustment of constituencies was carried out after the Census in 1961 and 1971. The delimitation based on the 1971 Census was completed in 1976. The Forty-Second Amendment of the Constitution froze further delimitation until the Census of 2001. It was intended to ensure that States successfully curbing population growth were not disadvantaged in terms of representation, while States with higher population growth did not gain a corresponding increase in seats. The temporary freeze on delimitation ended in 2001. However, the government decided to redraw the territories of constituencies to ensure inter se parity in terms of population across them. The Constitutional provisions were amended to provide that territories of the constituencies would be readjusted on the basis of the 2001 Census figures without altering the number of seats. The Statement of Objects and Reasons in the Bill for the Constitution (Eighty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2001 stated that the government decided to extend the freeze on undertaking fresh delimitation up to the year 2026. As per the provisions of Articles 82 and 170(3), the freeze on further delimitation is to be in place until the population figures of the first Census to be taken after 2026 are published. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the current Delimitation Bill, 2026 noted that population growth and migration "have resulted in varying density of population in electoral constituencies"; the Bill sought to address this issue. However, the population figures of the 2011 Census were to be adopted. There is nothing to suggest that migration has either stopped or slowed since 2011, or that population growth has stabilised uniformly across all regions. It was quite likely that when constituencies are finally carved out, many of them would exhibit real-time disparities when compared with the principles set out in the present Bill.

passages.text: The U.S. has allowed its waiver of sanctions on Iran's Chabahar port to lapse, indicating that India is now at a crossroads on how to proceed with the port as a key connectivity initiative. Barring a belated waiver renewal, New Delhi must choose between accepting sanctions and abandoning its $620 million investment, or proceeding with the project and risk strict U.S. sanctions. India's "start-stop" engagement with Iran on developing a facility at the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar goes back decades, and Prime Minister A.B. Vajpayee signed an MoU for the project in 2003. However, U.S. pressure on India to postpone plans aimed at stopping Iran's nuclear programme led to construction delays. The Manmohan Singh government was unable to make much progress either, but continued work on the Zaranj-Delaram highway to connect the Iran-Afghanistan border crossing to Kabul. After the 2015 JCPOA, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government signed a trilateral agreement with Iran and Afghanistan to advance trade and aid via Chabahar port and a highway into Afghanistan. Chabahar's importance grew as ties with Pakistan deteriorated and it restricted India's transit access to Afghanistan. However, fate intervened again as U.S. President Donald Trump walked out of the JCPOA, and began a "maximum pressure" campaign against Iran by re-implementing all sanctions. While India was forced by the U.S. to give up Iranian oil imports and plans for the rail line, the U.S. built a "carve-out" for Chabahar, allowing India to send wheat and medical supplies to Afghanistan. That carve-out is now at an end, with the Trump administration giving Delhi until this month to "wind-down" its operations. Since November 2025, India has withdrawn personnel from Chabahar, prepaid its $120 million investment commitment, and is considering transferring its stake in the Shahid Beheshti Terminal to an Iranian company. The West Asia war has complicated the situation, and it is unclear when India will be able to re-engage with Iran or rebuild Chabahar. Temporarily dropping the project may seem pragmatic. However, Chabahar is just one of several India's independent decisions that the U.S. has thwarted, including demands to stop buying oil from Iran, Venezuela, and Russia. Giving in on Chabahar will not just end India's connectivity plans with Iran, Central Asia and Afghanistan, but also damage its claims of sovereign autonomy and its ability to pursue an independent foreign policy. passages.text: In the centuries after A.D. 1500, as European explorers became aware of the wide differences among the world's peoples in technology and political organization, they assumed that those differences arose from differences in innate ability. With the rise of Darwinian theory, explanations were recast in terms of natural selection and of evolutionary descent. Technologically primitive peoples were considered evolutionary vestiges of human descent from apelike ancestors. The displacement of such peoples by colonists from industrialized societies exemplified the survival of the fittest. With the later rise of genetics, the explanations were recast once again, in genetic terms. Europeans became considered genetically more intelligent than Africans, and especially more so than Aboriginal Australians. Today, segments of Western society publicly repudiate racism. Yet many Westerners continue to accept racist explanations privately or subconsciously. Even educated white Americans, Europeans, and Australians, when the subject of Australian Aborigines comes up, assume that there is something primitive about the Aborigines themselves. Many of the living descendants of those Aborigines who survived the era of European colonization are now finding it difficult to succeed economically in white Australian society. A seemingly compelling argument goes as follows. White immigrants to Australia built a literate, industrialized, politically centralized, democratic state based on metal tools and on food production, all within a century of colonizing a continent where the Aborigines had been living as tribal hunter-gatherers without metal for at least 40,000 years. Here were two successive experiments in human development, in which the environment was identical and the sole variable was the people occupying that environment. The objection to such racist explanations is not just that they are loathsome, but also that they are wrong. Sound evidence for the existence of human differences in intelligence that parallel human differences in technology is lacking. Peoples who until recently were technologically primitive routinely master industrial technologies when given opportunities to do so. An enormous effort by cognitive psychologists has gone into the search for differences in IQ between peoples of different geographic origins now living in the same country. However, the peoples compared differ greatly in their social environment and educational opportunities. Even our cognitive abilities as adults are heavily influenced by the social environment that we experienced during childhood. Tests of cognitive ability tend to measure cultural learning and not pure innate intelligence. (384 words, source: https://newsroom.ucla.edu/)

passages.text: The Mahabodhi Temple stands as one of the most revered and historically layered monuments in the Buddhist world, embodying both spiritual awakening and architectural endurance. Located in Bodh Gaya, the site marks the exact spot where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment nearly 2,500 years ago. According to tradition, the young seeker meditated under a peepal tree for three days, culminating in a moment of profound realization that transformed him into the Buddha, or the "Enlightened One." Recognizing the sanctity of this event, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka commissioned the first shrine at this location in the 3rd century BCE, making it one of the earliest formal Buddhist monuments. Over time, however, the structure underwent several transformations. The present temple, with its soaring pyramidal tower rising approximately 55 metres, largely dates to the Gupta period (5th-6th century CE), a time often associated with artistic and architectural refinement in the Indian subcontinent. Beyond its historical origins, the temple complex is rich in symbolic elements. Adjacent to the shrine stands a descendant of the original Bodhi Tree, under which the Buddha meditated. At its base lies the Vajrasana, or "Diamond Throne," believed to mark the precise spot of enlightenment. The temple itself is enclosed by intricately carved stone railings, some dating back to the 2nd century BCE, depicting motifs from Buddhist lore and everyday life. Yet, the journey of the Mahabodhi Temple has not been uninterrupted. With the decline of Buddhism in India after the 8th century, the site gradually fell into neglect and even changed custodial hands. By the late 19th century, it required significant restoration, which was undertaken with the involvement of both Burmese patrons and British officials. A prolonged legal and religious struggle eventually restored its status as a Buddhist shrine, though its management continues to reflect a shared religious legacy. Today, the Mahabodhi Temple is not merely an architectural relic but a living centre of pilgrimage, drawing devotees from across the globe. Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002, it continues to resonate with spiritual vitality while bearing silent testimony to centuries of devotion, conflict, and renewal. passages.text: The rise of the Indian Writing in English is, at the onset, to be located historically. The first connection that we should be looking at is the introduction of the English language as a medium of instruction in India and the introduction of English literature as a subject in the Universities. Macaulay's Minute introduced in 1833 provided for the introduction of English as a medium of instruction with the claim that "the English tongue would be the most useful for our native subjects." While presenting his famous minute, Macaulay admitted quite candidly that he had not read any of the Sanskrit and Arabic books and yet did not desist from making such a pronouncement: "…A single shelf of a good European library is worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia. …All the historical information which has been collected in the Sanskrit language is less than what may be found in the paltry abridgements used at preparatory schools of England…" India, thus became a kind of testing ground for the launch of English literature in the classroom at a time when English Universities were still steeped in the Latin and Greek classics. English was, as a result, introduced in educational institutions, Courts and offices thus dislodging the traditional use of Arabic and Sanskrit as a mode of communication and documentation. Lord William Bentick announced in 1835 that the government would "favour English Language alone" henceforth and would move towards "a knowledge of English literature and Science through the medium of English language alone." The Wood Dispatch of 1854 proclaimed the establishment of the Universities at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta and thereafter made the English language accessible to students, professors and also the officials of Government offices. To begin with the introduction of English at these levels had some interesting repercussions. What is pejoratively called "Babu English" today became the first offspring of the unholy encounter between the British English language and the unwilling Babu. The 'art and craft' and discomfort with which they used the language in the offices in course became a matter of derision. In the arena of literary studies too English began to assert itself. passages.text: The anti-defection framework in India is governed by the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India, introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 and later strengthened by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. Its primary objective is to ensure stability in governance by discouraging opportunistic political defections. A legislator may incur disqualification if they voluntarily give up the membership of their political party, or if they vote or abstain from voting contrary to the party whip without prior permission. The expression "voluntarily giving up membership" has been interpreted broadly and is not confined to formal resignation; it may be inferred from conduct, public declarations, or alignment with rival political formations. Members who do not accept the merger are not deemed to have defected and may continue separately. The authority to decide disqualification petitions lies with the Speaker or Chairman of the House. passages.text: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, contingent contracts are governed by Sections 31 to 36. A contingent contract is a contract to do or not do something depending on the happening or non-happening of an uncertain future event, which must be collateral to the contract. The event should not form part of the reciprocal promises themselves but must be an independent condition upon which performance depends. Such contracts are enforceable only upon the occurrence (or non-occurrence) of the specified event. Where the contract depends on the happening of an event, it cannot be enforced until the event occurs. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Importantly, the impossibility must relate to the specific event contemplated by the parties, and not merely a similar or alternative occurrence. In cases where the contract depends on the non-happening of an event within a fixed time, the contract becomes enforceable when the time expires and the event has not occurred. However, if before the expiry of the specified time, the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes enforceable immediately, as the condition of non-happening is conclusively satisfied. Conversely, where the contract depends on the happening of an event within a fixed time, and such event becomes impossible before the expiry of that time, the contract becomes void immediately. Thus, the law distinguishes carefully between (i) contracts dependent on happening, (ii) contracts dependent on non-happening, and (iii) contracts tied to a specific time frame. A crucial principle is that the event must be construed strictly as agreed between the parties. If the contract specifies the occurrence of a particular event in a particular manner (for example, destruction by fire), the occurrence of a similar result by a different cause (such as demolition) will not satisfy the condition. A wager agreement, governed by Section 30, is an agreement where two parties agree that upon the determination of an uncertain event, one shall win and the other shall lose, and neither party has any interest in that event except the stake. Such agreements are void. The essential elements of a wager include mutual chance of gain and loss, absence of control over the event, and absence of any real or commercial interest in the occurrence of the event. The distinction between a contingent contract and a wager agreement lies primarily in the presence of a legitimate interest. Where a party stands to suffer loss or derive benefit independent of the stake (for instance, due to ownership, business interest, or financial exposure), the agreement is not treated as a wager, even though it may depend on an uncertain event. Courts, therefore, look beyond form and examine the substance of the transaction, particularly whether the uncertain event is merely collateral to a genuine transaction or constitutes the sole basis of the agreement.

passages.text: With the rapid growth of digital commerce, contracts formed through electronic means commonly known as e-contracts have gained legal recognition under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Indian Contract Act, 1872. An e-contract is formed through electronic communication, such as emails, clicks, or digital acceptance mechanisms, provided that the essential elements of a valid contract i.e., offer, acceptance, lawful consideration, and free consent are satisfied. Click-wrap agreements, where users explicitly click "I agree," are generally enforceable as they demonstrate clear consent. Browse-wrap agreements, where terms are merely posted on a website without requiring explicit acceptance, are enforceable only when the user has actual or constructive knowledge of the terms. Courts often scrutinize whether reasonable notice of such terms was provided. The validity of e-contracts also depends on proper communication of offer and acceptance. The "click" or electronic assent must be free, informed, and not induced by misrepresentation, coercion, or fraud. Where terms are hidden, misleading, or presented in a manner that a reasonable user would not notice, consent may be vitiated. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, consumers engaging in e-commerce transactions are entitled to protection against unfair trade practices, misleading advertisements, and defective goods or deficient services. E-commerce platforms may be classified either as intermediaries (facilitating transactions) or as sellers, depending on the degree of control exercised over the transaction. Liability often turns on this distinction. The Act recognizes rights such as the right to be informed, the right to seek redressal, and protection against unfair contracts. In digital transactions, obvious pricing errors or technical glitches (such as a product being listed at an unrealistically low price due to system error) may affect the validity of consent. Where a reasonable user would recognize the error, such apparent acceptance may not amount to genuine and informed consent. An unfair contract may include terms that are excessively one-sided, such as unilateral modification clauses, disproportionate penalties, or exclusion of liability for negligence. Additionally, digital transactions often raise issues regarding jurisdiction and standard form contracts. Courts may examine whether consumers had a meaningful opportunity to understand terms, whether the platform exercised dominance, and whether contractual clauses unfairly restrict consumer remedies. Thus, while e-contracts are valid, their enforceability is closely tied to transparency, fairness, and genuine consent, especially in consumer transactions.

passages.text: With the rapid rise of social media, influencer marketing has emerged as a dominant form of digital advertising. Influencers, who often command large and loyal audiences, promote products and services through posts, videos, and endorsements. However, this form of marketing raises significant legal concerns, particularly when endorsements are misleading or not transparently disclosed. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, misleading advertisements are prohibited. An advertisement is considered misleading if it falsely describes a product, gives false guarantees, or conceals material information. Influencers who endorse products without disclosing material connections-such as paid partnerships, sponsorships, or free products-may contribute to such misleading practices. The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has issued guidelines requiring influencers to clearly disclose paid promotions using terms such as "#ad" or "#sponsored." Failure to do so may attract liability, not only for the brand but also for the influencer, especially if the endorsement affects consumer decision-making. At the same time, liability depends on the role played by each party. Brands are generally responsible for the claims made about their products. However, influencers may also be held liable if they make false representations or fail to exercise due diligence before endorsing a product. Due diligence requires that influencers have a reasonable basis for believing the claims they make. These principles intersect with contract law under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, particularly in relation to misrepresentation and free consent. If consumers rely on influencer endorsements that are misleading, their consent to purchase may be considered vitiated. Courts and regulators increasingly emphasize that digital advertising must ensure transparency, fairness, and accountability.The key question is not merely whether an endorsement exists, but whether it misleads a reasonable consumer into making a decision they would not have otherwise made.

passages.text: Under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the right of private defence is recognised as a natural right allowing individuals to protect their body and property against unlawful aggression. Sections 96 to 106 provide that an act done in the exercise of this right is not an offence, provided it falls within prescribed limits. The right arises when there is a reasonable apprehension of danger to body or property. It is not necessary that the offence be actually committed; the apprehension itself must be real and immediate. However, the right is preventive and not punitive-it cannot be exercised as retaliation after the danger has ceased. The extent of this right depends on the nature of the threat. In certain circumstances, the right extends to causing death, particularly where the assault reasonably causes apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, kidnapping, or wrongful confinement. However, the force used must be proportionate to the threat perceived. The law imposes clear limitations. The right cannot be exercised against acts done by public servants acting in good faith under colour of office, unless there is reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. Further, the right does not extend to situations where there is sufficient time to seek protection from public authorities.Another important limitation is that the harm caused in private defence must not be more than necessary. If the defender exceeds this limit, the protection is lost, and criminal liability may arise depending on the intention and circumstances. In assessing such cases, courts examine whether the accused acted in good faith, whether the apprehension was reasonable, and whether the response was proportionate. The law thus balances the need for self-preservation with the broader objective of preventing misuse of defensive rights.

passages.text: Will the Tech Takeover lead to public reaction against these intrusive new technologies being pushed into our lives by the fusing of government and corporate power?... We're beginning to see the stirrings of minor rebellion against the Tech Takeover. The only problem is, unlike the Wizard of Oz, there appears to be no one behind the curtain to identify. That's because the Tech Takeover is being orchestrated on multiple levels and by multiple players. Further, the technology itself is being embedded in every nook and cranny of our lives with too many examples to enumerate in this article. People who live in apartments now sometimes need to use a smartphone simply to do laundry in their buildings or park in the town parking lot. As helpful as smartphones can at times be, this represents a new kind of economic discrimination towards the elderly and financially distressed and is just one example of deepening technological dependency. In the 80's and 90's, science fiction movies and literature commonly had themes of "robot wars" where humans were pitted against the dominance of a robotic society. Will this be our future? Will there be a mass uprising against AI and the vast AI-based robotic machinery that's taking over both the means of production and the means of information? We humans are known for our adaptability and stoicism in difficult situations such as world wars and major disasters. That stoicism and sense of "accepting what can't be changed" seems to be part of our psychological and perhaps even biological makeup. But the tech takeover is such a massive appropriation of our social, political, and cultural life --- and indeed our own biological substrate --- that stoic acceptance might not be the way to go. In the next few years, it most certainly will have finally dawned on the mass of humanity especially in advanced Western nations that something is badly amiss. Many will realize at a visceral level that their everyday lives are trapped in a claustrophobia-inducing closed- circuit technocratic system that robs them of autonomy and freedom while purporting to do the opposite. While-wisely adopted-emerging technologies still offers great promise, many aspects of the technology that Big Tech promised would advance the quality of our lives has arguably turned out to be a grand illusion and an existential trap. It has been perpetrated by an out-of- control combination of government and corporate interests and a few unelected oligarchs that have a surfeit of power that no one or no institution can seem to contain.By 2025, it's quite possible we'll see the beginning of the "robot wars" in which humanity, at least on some level, begins to push back against the unyielding juggernaut of the Tech Takeover.

passages.text: In the years before Lehman Brothers went bust in 2008, plunging the world into financial crisis, macroeconomists were understandably worried. But they worried about the wrong thing: not over-indebted American banks, but over-thrifty Asian economies. According to this theory, Asia's determination to accumulate dollar reserves was depressing interest rates, tempting Americans to overspend. The upshot was that Asia earned more than it spent, resulting in large trade surpluses. This enabled America to spend more than it earned, reflected in a yawning current-account deficit. These "global imbalances" are back. The new imbalances are not quite as big as those of two decades ago. The world's deficit countries had a combined current-account gap of 1.6% of global GDP in 2025, compared with a peak of 2.6% in 2006. President Donald Trump cited America's deficit to justify his "Liberation Day" tariffs last year. President Emmanuel Macron of France called China's surpluses "unbearable" on his visit to Beijing in December. One answer is America's budget deficit. Tax cuts or higher welfare spending increase American consumption and reduce saving. That can lift interest rates and thus the dollar-which makes exports less competitive, deepening the trade deficit. Other commentators are equally confident that the culprit is once again Asia, especially China. China subsidises its manufacturers, resulting in excess capacity. What these firms cannot sell at home, they dump abroad. This crowds out local manufacturers, destroying jobs and obliging countries like America to increase their fiscal deficits to restore demand and curb unemployment. What has suppressed domestic spending in China is a property slump. If China is the culprit for imbalances, it has perpetrated more a blunder than a crime. Its big fiscal deficits are a political choice not an economic necessity. The causes of global imbalances are not, then, as clear as some commentators allege. All of the suspects are implicated. But the ending could still be bad.

passages.text: In her essay "The Gentle Leviathan", Niraja Gopal Jayal argues that by separating the non-justiciable welfare commitments from the enforceable "liberty rights" of Part III, the Constitution grounded welfare in a language of state responsibility tempered by discretion. "The Indian state adheres to a needs-based conception of justice in theory," she observes, "but in practice follows a philosophy of welfare manifestly based in ideas of charity and benevolence. The idea of a right to welfare is clearly precluded". Income transfers and subsidies, therefore, are not sudden political inventions; they are contemporary instruments through which an older constitutional commitment to social and economic justice is expressed. There are, however, important differences between welfare in its classical sense-echoed in the Constitution-and what is today described as the "new" welfare associated with freebies. In its classical conception, welfare was understood as structurally integral to liberal capitalism. John Maynard Keynes anticipated that public and private investment could sustain a high and stable level of employment, wages, and effective demand. If profits were reinvested rather than hoarded, growth would expand the economic pie in ways that supported both accumulation and social provisioning. Early experiments in India partly moved in this direction. In Tamil Nadu, K. Kamaraj expanded free education and school meals from the late 1950s. The promise of heavily subsidised rice by C.N. Annadurai in 1967 marked a decisive shift: welfare became not only developmental policy but also a visible political claim. Around the same time, Kerala moved towards near-universal schooling through extensive public provisioning and regulation of aided schools well before education was recognised nationally as a fundamental right. Maharashtra's Employment Guarantee Scheme of the early 1970s, conceived partly to provide rural employment and slow distress migration to Bombay, offered another example of welfare tied directly to the creation of work rather than simple transfers, anticipating later national programmes such as the MGNREGA (Echeverri-Gent 1988). In these early initiatives, welfare was tied to the expansion of capabilities and public services, reinforcing attempts to steer capitalism in a more humane direction. If classical welfare sought to integrate citizens into the productive economy as rights-bearing members, the "new" welfare operates through the idiom of beneficiaries or labharthis dependent on the benefactor's largesse. Entitlements grounded in universal rights and systematic public provisioning give way to targeted distributions of private goods such as cycles, laptops, televisions, or cash transfers. Enabled by digital identification and direct bank credits, welfare can now be finely individuated even when directed at specific classes or communities.

passages.text: A retail store sells five items — laptops, smartphones, headphones, tablets, and smartwatches. Each item is strategically priced by marking it above the cost price and then offering discounts to attract customers. A profit is earned when the selling price exceeds the cost price, while a loss occurs when heavy discounts reduce the selling price below the cost price. High-demand items, such as smartphones, often provide better profit margins, whereas accessories may be discounted more aggressively. By balancing discounts and profit margins, the store aims to maximize overall profit while remaining competitive. Careful pricing ensures sustainability, customer satisfaction, and steady revenue growth in a competitive market. The laptop has a marked price of Rs. 65,000, and after offering a discount of 20%, the shopkeeper earns a profit of Rs. 2,000. The cost price of the smartwatch is half the cost price of the tablet, and after selling the smartwatch at a discount of 40% on the marked price, the shopkeeper incurs a loss of 10%. The tablet is sold for Rs. 23,800 after a discount of 15% on the marked price, and the shopkeeper earns a profit of 19%. The cost price of the smartphone is equal to the sum of the cost prices of the tablet and the smartwatch. The shopkeeper marks the smartphone at 40% above its cost price, and after offering a discount on the marked price, he earns a profit of 5%. The headphone is marked 50% above the cost price, and by selling it for Rs. 4,200, the shopkeeper earns a profit of 5%.

passages.text: Constitutional democracies do not merely protect the right to speak; they create conditions under which disagreement can survive. Liberty of thought and expression is valuable not only because it protects individual autonomy but because it enables competing visions of society to coexist. Fraternity, one of the values recognised in the constitutional framework, requires citizens to acknowledge one another as equal participants despite differences in belief, ideology, faith, or social identity. It therefore accommodates disagreement and discourages enforced conformity. Throughout history, free speech has often enabled individuals and groups lacking social or political power to participate in democratic discourse. Reform movements seeking equality, dignity, and inclusion have frequently depended upon speech and expression to challenge existing structures. Therefore, dissenting opinions cannot ordinarily be suppressed merely because they disturb dominant opinion or unsettle prevailing social norms. However, constitutional protection of speech does not imply complete immunity. Freedom of expression may be subject to restrictions where expression threatens constitutionally recognised interests such as public order, decency, morality, security of the State, or the dignity of particular communities. Yet restrictions imposed upon speech must satisfy the principle of proportionality. The mere existence of disagreement or discomfort does not justify broad restrictions. Measures adopted must bear a rational connection with the objective sought and should interfere with speech only to the extent necessary. Constitutional values also distinguish between constitutional morality and popular morality. Popular morality may reflect majoritarian beliefs, customs, or social attitudes prevailing at a given time. Constitutional morality, however, derives from principles of equality, dignity, liberty, and justice embedded within the constitutional order. Constitutional rights cannot ordinarily be denied merely because a majority of people disagree with a particular belief or expression. Furthermore, threats to free expression may arise not only through direct governmental action but also through organised private conduct. If private groups use intimidation, social pressure, economic retaliation, or coordinated harassment to silence unpopular views, the practical value of free speech may become illusory. In such circumstances, the State may possess a positive obligation not merely to avoid suppressing expression itself, but also to ensure that individuals are not effectively prevented from exercising their constitutional freedoms. Finally, constitutional values are often best assessed from the standpoint of those who remain vulnerable or excluded from dominant structures. Justice and equality cannot be evaluated merely through the experiences of those who already possess social or economic privilege. Constitutionalism frequently requires attention to the perspectives of those whose voices remain unheard.

passages.text: Negligence originates from the Latin term “negligentia,” meaning “failure to pick up” or “neglect.” At its core, negligence refers to carelessness or a failure to exercise the degree of care that a reasonable person would, resulting in harm to another. To establish negligence, several essential elements must be proved. First, there must be a duty of care, meaning the defendant must owe a legal obligation to act with reasonable caution toward the plaintiff. This duty arises when one person’s actions may reasonably and foreseeably affect another’s safety, and its existence depends on the relationship between the parties. Secondly, there must be a breach of duty, which occurs when the defendant fails to act as a reasonable person would under similar circumstances. The standard of care is assessed objectively by comparing the defendant’s conduct to that of an ordinarily prudent person. Another requirement is causation, meaning the breach of duty must directly result in harm to the plaintiff. Causation consists of two components. The first is actual or factual causation, commonly assessed using the “but for” test, which asks whether the harm would have occurred but for the defendant’s act. The second is legal or proximate causation, which examines whether the harm was a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the defendant’s actions. Further, the plaintiff must establish damage, demonstrating that actual injury or loss resulted from the defendant’s negligence. Foreseeability also plays an important role in negligence law, as the harm suffered must have been reasonably foreseeable at the time of the negligent act. A person generally cannot be held liable for highly unusual or remote consequences that could not reasonably have been anticipated. The law also adopts an objective standard through the reasonable person standard, which asks how an ordinarily prudent individual would have acted in the same situation. Personal limitations or characteristics of the defendant, such as carelessness or inexperience, are generally not considered relevant in determining liability. Certain defenses may also be available in negligence actions. One such defense is contributory negligence, which arises when the plaintiff contributes to his or her own harm by failing to take reasonable care for personal safety. In such situations, although the defendant may have acted negligently, the plaintiff’s own negligence may reduce or completely bar recovery of damages. Another defense is an Act of God (Vis Major), which refers to extraordinary natural events beyond human control or foresight that cannot be prevented despite reasonable care. Since such events are unforeseeable and irresistible, the defendant is generally not held liable if the harm resulted solely from them. Closely related is the concept of an inevitable accident, which refers to an event that could not have been prevented despite the exercise of reasonable care, caution, and skill. Unlike an Act of God, an inevitable accident may arise from human conduct rather than natural forces. Finally, the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur, meaning “the thing speaks for itself,” serves as a rule of evidence in negligence cases. It applies where the precise cause of an accident may be unknown, but the nature of the incident itself strongly suggests that it could not ordinarily have occurred without negligence. Source: https://www.manupatracademy.com

passages.text: Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person, or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver to any person property or valuable security, or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable security, commits “extortion.” Its aim, akin to blackmail, involves dishonestly obtaining payments or benefits from someone by instilling fear through threats. It occupies a middle ground between theft and robbery. The key components of extortion include intentionally inducing fear in a person and dishonestly persuading them, under that fear, to surrender property or valuable assets to another individual. A person must be put in fear of injury. To qualify as fear under extortion, it must be of such intensity as to disrupt the person’s mental composure and deprive them of free consent. In extortion cases, the validity of the accusation is irrelevant; the mere threat of harm, whether physical or reputational, constitutes an offence. The term “injury” encompasses harm to body, mind, reputation, or property. Dishonest inducement is another crucial aspect of extortion and lies in the dishonest inducement. Mere causing of wrongful loss is insufficient; there must be an intention on the part of the individual instilling fear to cause wrongful loss or gain. The delivery of property or valuable security by the person put in fear to another person is also essential. For extortion to occur, there must be documented threat or fear of injury compelling the victim to surrender property to the perpetrator. This fear-induced surrender is essential for the offence. Criminal activities like extortion and robbery are often misunderstood due to their overlapping elements. However, these crimes are distinct in their methods, impacts, and legal consequences. Extortion relies on threats and psychological manipulation to unlawfully obtain money or property, while robbery involves direct force or intimidation, often in the victim’s immediate presence. Robbery involves the direct and unlawful taking of someone’s property by using force or intimidation. Unlike extortion, robbery typically occurs in the presence of the victim and involves immediate threats or acts of physical violence. Source: https://www.defactojudiciary.in

passages.text: A seller is deemed to be an unpaid seller under certain conditions. Firstly, a seller is considered unpaid if the whole price of the goods sold has not been paid or tendered. Secondly, a seller may also be regarded as unpaid where a bill of exchange or any other negotiable instrument has been accepted as conditional payment, but the condition remains unfulfilled due to dishonour of the instrument or otherwise. An unpaid seller possesses certain rights against the goods sold. One such right is the Right of Lien. The right of lien permits an unpaid seller to retain possession of the goods until payment is made. This right may be exercised where the goods are sold without any credit terms, where the credit period has expired, or where the buyer becomes insolvent. Lien is regarded as a “particular lien,” meaning it can be exercised only by the seller and not by any assignee or creditor. The seller may exercise this right even if the goods are held as an agent or bailee of the buyer. Another important right is the Right of Stoppage in Transit. This right enables the unpaid seller to stop the goods from being delivered to the buyer and to regain possession while the goods are still in transit. However, this right becomes available only when the buyer becomes insolvent after the sale. Goods are regarded as being in transit from the time they are delivered to a carrier until the buyer or the buyer’s agent takes delivery. The unpaid seller also enjoys the Right of Resale. Where the goods are perishable in nature, the seller may resell them without providing notice to the buyer. However, where the goods are non-perishable, the seller must provide notice to the buyer and allow a reasonable period for payment before reselling them. Further, the seller may also resell where an express right of resale has been reserved in the contract itself. If the seller resells the goods without giving the required notice, the seller cannot recover damages from the buyer for losses suffered due to the resale. However, where proper notice has been given, the seller may claim damages and also retain any profit arising from the resale. It is important to distinguish between the right of lien and the right of stoppage in transit. The right of lien remains available only so long as the unpaid seller continues to retain possession of the goods. In contrast, the right of stoppage in transit arises only after the seller has parted with possession of the goods, while they are still in the course of transit. Source: https://www.defactolaw.in/post

passages.text: Contracts are founded upon the principle that parties who voluntarily enter into legally enforceable agreements are expected to perform the obligations they have undertaken. Ordinarily, a mere increase in difficulty, inconvenience, expense, or hardship does not excuse a party from performance. However, the law recognises certain situations in which performance may become impossible or fundamentally different from what the parties originally contemplated. This principle is generally referred to as the doctrine of frustration. Frustration arises when, after the formation of a valid contract and without fault of either party, an unforeseen event occurs that renders performance impossible, unlawful, or radically different from what the parties intended at the time of contracting. Such events may include destruction of the subject matter, change in law, death or incapacity in contracts requiring personal skill, or cancellation of an event that forms the foundation of the agreement. However, frustration cannot be invoked where the event was foreseeable, where the parties themselves created the impossibility, or where performance merely became more expensive, less profitable, or commercially inconvenient. When frustration occurs, the contract is automatically discharged and parties are released from future obligations. However, obligations already performed prior to frustration may continue to have legal consequences. Distinct from frustration is breach of contract, which occurs when a party fails to perform a contractual obligation without lawful excuse. Breach may be actual or anticipatory. An actual breach occurs where a party refuses or fails to perform when performance becomes due. For example, if a supplier fails to deliver goods on the agreed date, the breach occurs on that date itself. An anticipatory breach occurs when, before the time fixed for performance arrives, one party either expressly communicates an intention not to perform the contract or acts in a manner making performance impossible. Upon anticipatory breach, the innocent party generally has two options. First, the innocent party may immediately treat the contract as terminated and sue for damages. Second, the innocent party may elect to keep the contract alive and wait until the date of performance. However, if the innocent party chooses to keep the contract alive and a frustrating event occurs before the performance date, the contract may subsequently be discharged by frustration, potentially affecting the right to damages. The law also distinguishes between self-induced impossibility and genuine frustration. A party cannot deliberately create circumstances preventing performance and later rely upon frustration to escape liability. Thus, if impossibility results from a party’s own actions, the matter is treated as breach rather than frustration.

passages.text: Question: You have had an unusually eventful term so far. Donald Trump’s tariffs, whose weight India has felt unfairly, have shaken global trade. The rupee has fallen sharply. So has inflation, to a multi-year low. Yet India clocked 8.2 percent GDP growth in Q2FY26. You have called it a Goldilocks phase for the Indian economy. What did you mean? In economic terms, Goldilocks phase is the balance of growth and inflation. Usually, high growth leads to high inflation, and low inflation is accompanied by low growth. But we are having the best of both worlds-low inflation and high growth. That’s a sweet spot to be in. Question: Are we genuinely in a structurally strong phase of growth or is this a window created by a unique alignment of global and domestic factors? Despite the external headwinds of geopolitical events, tensions and trade fragmentation, the Indian economy, in the first three quarters for which we have data this calendar year, has done remarkably well, both in terms of inflation, where we are at historic lows, and in growth, where we have averaged about 8 percent. Going forward, for FY26, we are projecting growth of 7.3 percent, and for the next two quarters of FY27, 6.7 and 6.8 percent, respectively. Frankly, it’s very difficult to precisely forecast what the numbers will be over a long period. But, yes, this sets the stage for India to do well. Question: Since February 2025, the RBI has cut the policy rate by 125 basis points (bps). It is now 5.25 percent. This is striking because the last comparable easing happened in 2019 or so when there was a sharp slowdown in growth. This time, rates have been cut despite high GDP growth. What has changed in the RBI’s assessment? The last time we brought down rates to as low as 5.25 percent, and then even further down to 4 percent, we were in a different situation- growth was low and inflation high, with headline inflation more than 4 percent in 2021. This time around, growth is good and inflation benign. Monetary policy is always forward-looking and with inflation projected at 3.5 percent or so and growth expected to moderate over the next two quarters, the policy repo rates were lowered. Question: And going forward? Monetary policy is not preset, it is evolving. We are data-dependent. We are in a neutral phase. It is for the MPC (Monetary Policy Committee) to see what the data points are and what we should be doing. However, as I mentioned, I do feel inflation will remain benign for a long time. And if that is so, barring shocks on the supply side, the weather, geopolitics or something else, we’re in for a long period of low policy rates.

passages.text: A commercial jet zooming at 500 knots (575mph) and the stately progress of a tanker cruising at 15 knots yield journey times from the Persian Gulf to Europe measured either in hours or weeks. The difference belies a fundamental connection. The near complete closure of the Strait of Hormuz has prevented both jet fuel and the crude oil from which it is refined from exiting the Gulf, sending prices into a rapid climb. Since the conflict with Iran began, the cost of filling up a plane has thus soared. That has already claimed one corporate victim. Spirit Airlines, an American low-cost carrier in bankruptcy protection, ceased operating on May 2nd. Its finances buckled under the weight of rising fuel costs. Other airlines have put up ticket prices, added fuel surcharges and cancelled flights that would no longer have been profitable. Among those to have cut flights are Lufthansa, Air France-klm, United, Delta, Vietjet and AirAsia. Further down the runway, however, the number of flights is still set to increase by 3-6% in the summer compared with last year. That hardly accords with the availability of jet fuel. Demand averaged around 7.8m barrels per day in 2025, according to Société Générale, with 360,000 b/d coming through the Strait of Hormuz. What explains the disconnect between looming shortages and expanding schedules? As Andrew Charlton of Aviation Advocacy explains, the last thing to change will be “optimistic messages” from airlines that need to keep selling tickets to maintain cashflow. America, the world’s biggest aviation market, should on the whole remain well supplied. Yet it is not entirely immune. Stocks are running down on the West Coast, which relies partly on imports from South Korea, now struggling with the loss of crude from the Gulf. Britain, which has no strategic reserve, now has a stock of just 29 days of jet fuel, according to Goldman Sachs. For Portugal the figure has fallen to 23 days, a level at which rationing may be required. As the busy summer season approaches, it is difficult to tell whose holidays will be spoiled by the jet-fuel shortage. It would be no surprise if a few more carriers follow Spirit to the afterlife.
