passages.text: As geopolitical tensions expose the risks of over-dependence on one 'factory of the world', global firms are diversifying. The 'China+1' mantra is propelling capital towards alternatives. India looks primed to gain - on paper. The pitch is seductive: the planet's most populous country, with a young workforce and huge market, ready to wrest manufacturing from a slowing China beset by anaemic demand, deflation and a weak housing market. Yet interviews by National University of Singapore's East Asian Institute with 50 executives, officials and experts across India, America and Singapore and official data paint a more cautious picture. The shift from China to India is no stampede, but a slow shuffle shaped by India's enduring obstacles as much as by its opportunities. China+1 is not about decoupling; global supply chains remain entwined with China. For most multinationals, India is a complement, not a substitute. Apple expands in India but retains its vast Chinese operations. Firms cling to China for high-end manufacturing, R&D and its domestic market, while spreading lower-end production elsewhere for resilience. India has notched gains. Gross foreign direct investment hit $81bn in 2024-25, up 14% year-on-year. Production-linked incentive schemes have lured factories from electronics to pills. Pharma alone generated sales of 2.66trn rupees ($28.1bn) in three years under PLI, with exports of 1.7trn rupees and local value-added hitting 83.7% by March 2025. In Tamil Nadu, Foxconn and Apple's suppliers are clustering and growing, aided by swift, single-window approvals. When India's bureaucracy works, it works fast. America's tariffs - now hitting Indian goods alongside Chinese - have sharpened the urgency for India to build self-reliant supply chains. But harsh realities persist. India trails China not on headline costs but on reliability and supplier depth. Official logistics costs are around 8% of GDP. Bosses say the lived experience - delays, clunky multimodal links, and unpredictability - is costlier. Power tariffs roughly match China's on paper, but disruptions force firms to run costly diesel backups. Trucking 1,500km takes eight days, an aeon for just-in-time chains. Above all, India lacks China's dense web of parts-makers. (Source: The telegraph)

passages.text: It's the stuff of science fiction cinema, or particularly breathless AI company blogposts: new research finds recent AI systems can independently copy themselves on to other computers. In the doom scenario, this means that when the superintelligent AI goes rogue, it will escape shutdown by seeding itself across the world wide web, lurking outside the reach of frantic IT professionals and continuing to plot world domination or paving over the world with solar panels. "We're rapidly approaching the point where no one would be able to shut down a rogue AI, because it would be able to self-exfiltrate its weights and copy itself to thousands of computers around the world," said Jeffrey Ladish, the director of Palisade research, a Berkeley- based organisation which did the study. Like many of these advances, there are caveats to what Palisade found. Moreover, experts say it is unlikely that the AI systems they tested could accomplish the same thing, unnoticed, in real-world environments. "They are testing in environments that are like soft jelly in many cases," said Jamieson O'Reilly, an expert in offensive cybersecurity. "That doesn't take away from the value of their research, but it does mean the outcome might look far less scary in a real enterprise environment with even a medium level of monitoring," he added. Palisade tested several AI models in a controlled environment of networked computers. It gave the models a prompt to find and exploit vulnerabilities, and to use these to copy themselves from one computer to another. The models were able to do this, but not on every attempt. While a lot of computer viruses can already do this - copy themselves on to new computers - this is likely the first time an AI model has been shown capable of exploiting vulnerabilities to copy itself onto a new server, said O'Reilly. "Malware has been moving copies of itself around for decades, it's just that no one has done this in the wild, as far as I know, with local [large language models]." However, what Palisade documented has been technically possible for months, he added. "Palisade is the first to formally document it end-to-end in a paper. While not taking away from the research, they did the writing-up, not the unlocking." (Source: The Gurdian)

passages.text: India-US trade negotiations are currently marked by uncertainty due to unpredictable tariff policies adopted by the United States. According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), this instability creates the risk that India may enter an unequal trade agreement if safeguards against sudden tariff changes are not built into the deal. A key concern is that US tariff policy is both volatile and legally contested. Several tariff measures face judicial scrutiny within the United States, meaning they may remain in force, be overturned, or be modified unpredictably. This creates a situation where trade rules can shift even after agreements are signed, making long-term commitments fragile and unreliable. GTRI argues that this creates a structural imbalance in negotiating power. The United States can use tariff threats as leverage, while India may be forced to make immediate concessions to secure market access. However, the benefits India receives may be uncertain or conditional. Such asymmetry generally favours stronger economies, especially when negotiations occur under geopolitical pressure or urgency. Supporters of trade engagement argue that even imperfect agreements can generate benefits for India. These include better integration into global supply chains and improved export opportunities in manufacturing and services. They also suggest that tariff volatility in major economies may encourage firms to diversify investments toward relatively stable economies like India. Critics, however, argue that this optimism overlooks structural risks. If tariff regimes can change unilaterally, market access becomes conditional rather than guaranteed. This may lead to repeated renegotiations, weakening India's long-term bargaining position and increasing dependency over time. The debate reflects a broader shift in global trade governance. The ability of multilateral institutions to constrain unilateral economic action is weakening as protectionist policies gain political support in major economies. As a result, countries must balance short-term economic opportunities with long-term strategic autonomy and stability. Ultimately, the core dilemma is whether India should prioritise immediate economic gains through rapid trade agreements or insist on stronger safeguards to protect against future uncertainty. The outcome of this choice will shape not only India-US trade relations but also India's broader position in a fragmented global economic order. (Source: Economic Times)

passages.text: Sami trains in the alley off Al-Wahda Street, in Gaza, lifting chunks of concrete above his head, deadlifting car doors, and doing pull-ups from the frames of bombed-out windows. There is no gym anymore - only the skeletal remains of a neighborhood and a few iron bars salvaged from the wreckage. He keeps a pair of tattered training gloves in his pocket, a gift from his cousin Yusuf, who was killed in an airstrike. The gloves are split at the seams and darkened by sweat. He turns them over sometimes, as if inspecting a wound. Before the war, Sami had a routine. He worked part-time at a hardware shop, portioned his meals with surgical precision - eggs, chicken, rice - and saved for months to buy imported protein powder, clutching each tin like treasure. He trained at a gym near the beach until his shirt clung to him like a second skin. His dream was not fame or escape. It was simple: to grow bigger, to carve himself into something unbreakable. Now the chicken is gone. The eggs are scarce. He eats lentils, bread when there's bread, sardines from dented cans. He once found a row of canned sardines in the charred remains of Abu Khalil's Minimarket, clawing through plaster dust and shattered glass to reach them. That haul lasted him two weeks. He records everything in a notebook tucked into the sole of an old boot - reps, sets, rough calorie guesses - the ink running from sweat, but written nonetheless. On a WhatsApp call, he angled the phone so the narrator could read one entry: "Deadlift: 7 reps, 60 kg (I think - maybe more). Food: 100g lentils." There is a boy named Khaled - barefoot, maybe ten - who watches Sami lift and asks, "Why do you still do it?" Sami grins and says, "Because I can." But after Khaled walks away, something twists in Sami's chest. He wonders if lifting is theft - strength stolen from those who can't. Yet each time the bar digs into his shoulders, the shame burns off. He thinks: maybe what he offers is simply the sight of someone who hasn't quit. Maybe that is enough. The narrator closes with Camus: One must imagine Sisyphus happy. To bulk, to build, to lift - when the world wants you erased - is its own kind of refusal. Sami pushes the rock up the hill. It falls. He grips it again. (Source: Guernica magazine)

passages.text: After fifteen years of being a pair, Tashina craved to feel different. In her mind, she deserved the John Wayne jacket. For one, she knew more about it. While Krishauna was doing art and reading her anime books in the school library, she was on her school-issued Chromebook looking up John Wayne and discovered how while he was on set of the 1956 film The Searchers, a two-year-old Navajo child came down with pneumonia. Unable to get proper medical attention to her in time, John Wayne lent his plane and private pilot to the little girl and her family so they could get to the hospital. And that's how he got his name "The Man With The Big Eagle," from the Monument Valley Navajo extras. When Tashina watched The Searchers, John Wayne's character, Ethan Edwards, was scary to her. His character was a Civil War veteran who spent years searching for his niece, Debbie, after her family was killed and she was kidnapped by the Comanche. It confused Tashina how Edwards spent so much of the film searching for Debbie only to get pissed off when he found her living peacefully among the Comanche. He'd rather kill her than see her assimilated? She couldn't reconcile the John Wayne who could play a racist veteran who sided with the Confederacy, with the John Wayne who lent his plane to a sick little girl's family. Against the familiar backdrop of Monument Valley and orchestral fanfare, Tashina struggled to reconcile her lived reality with the rough and tumble fantasy of Edwards vying to exact revenge on the Comanche, a southern plains tribe, in Utah's arid deserts. How was it that they had his jacket, when everything surrounding his body of work and his behavior towards Natives, diverged so heavily from the Man With The Big Eagle story? From deep within her another question bubbled forth: who did the Big Eagle story benefit and was it even true? The jacket, Tashina thought suddenly, bolting up out of bed. Where the hell was the jacket?

passages.text: The Lok Sabha has taken up three bills, namely the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, the Delimitation Bill, 2026, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 for consideration and passing. The three legislations are intended to increase the participation of women in the Lok Sabha and the assemblies of States and Union Territories. The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, popularly known as Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, provided for the reservation of nearly one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and the legislative assemblies. The objective of the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam was to ensure greater participation of women in the democratic polity. These three bills have been brought to facilitate the delimitation of territorial constituencies and operationalise the provisions providing for the reservation of one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and legislative assemblies. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026, which has been introduced by Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal in the Lower House today, is intended to increase the number of seats in the Lok Sabha from 543 to [1]. Out of [1] seats, 815 members will be elected from the States and 35 members from the Union territories. The objective of the bill is to implement one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha as well as the assemblies of States and Union Territories. Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam which was passed in 2023 provided that one-third reservation for women will come into effect after the delimitation exercise based on the first census after the commencement of the Act. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill 2026 states that the next census and the consequential delimitation exercise will take considerable time, thus restricting effective and dedicated participation of women in the democratic polity. The objective of the bill is to operationalise one-third reservation for women through delimitation exercise based on the latest published census.

passages.text: The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in [1] by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) under the regulatory oversight of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), has emerged as the backbone of India’s digital payments ecosystem and a critical driver of financial inclusion. Over a decade of operations, UPI has demonstrated extraordinary scale and momentum. Annual transaction volume expanded from just 2 crore transactions in FY 2016-17 to over 24,162 crore transactions in FY 2025-26, representing an almost 12,000 fold surge in transaction volume. Parallelly, transaction value rose sharply from Rs. 0.07 lakh crore in FY 2016-17 to approximately Rs. 314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, translating into a more than 4,000 fold increase in transaction value. This simultaneous expansion in both volume and value highlights UPI’s deepening role in supporting high frequency retail payments. The unprecedented scale, reliability, and interoperability achieved by UPI have received global recognition, with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) acknowledging it as the world’s largest real time payment system by transaction volume, underscoring India’s leadership in building scalable, inclusive, and innovative digital public infrastructure. The Year 2025 marked a significant milestone in the growth trajectory of the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). Monthly transaction volumes crossed 2,000 crore transactions for the first time in August 2025, reaching 2,001 crore transactions, signalling a new scale of adoption. This momentum continued through the remainder of the year, with December 2025 recording 2,163 crore transactions, the highest monthly transaction volume in UPI’s decade long journey. Over the course of the calendar year 2025, UPI processed approximately 22,000 crore transactions in total, translating into a daily average of about 60 crore transactions. This sustained high frequency usage reflects the deep penetration of digital payments across the country and the growing trust of citizens, merchants, and businesses in India’s digital payments ecosystem.

passages.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin expressed confidence in Russia’s victory in Ukraine while overseeing the Victory Day military parade at Red Square, marking the 81st anniversary of the victory over Nazi Germany in World War II. Several foreign leaders also attended the ceremony. Addressing the gathering on Saturday, Mr. Putin praised Russian troops fighting in Ukraine, saying they were confronting an aggressive force armed and supported by the entire NATO bloc. The parade was held without tanks, missiles, or other heavy military equipment for the first time in nearly two decades, apart from a traditional flyover by combat jets. Russian officials said the sudden change in format was due to the current operational situation and heightened security concerns over possible Ukrainian attacks. The parade also featured troops from North Korea for the first time, as a tribute to Pyongyang that sent its soldiers to fight alongside Moscow forces against Ukraine.

passages.text: Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shri Bhupender Yadav announced the designation of Shekha Jheel Bird Sanctuary in Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh, as a Ramsar site, taking India’s total to 99 and the State’s tally to 12. “Uttar Pradesh takes the score to 99! Delighted to announce the designation of Shekha Jheel Bird Sanctuary (Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh) as a Ramsar site”, the Minister informed in a social media post. He said the announcement brings a boost for local livelihoods and global biodiversity, along with water and climate security and marks “India’s 99th, bringing us closer to a historic century”. “With PM Shri @narendramodi ji leading India’s ecosystem restoration mission, our commitment towards conservation of wetlands and natural habitat of animals, particularly that of birds, has yet again received a thumbs up from the global community,” the Minister added. Highlighting the ecological importance of the site, Shri Yadav said Shekha Jheel acts as a crucial stopover on the Central Asian Flyway, providing a vital habitat for migratory birds such as the Bar-headed Goose, Painted Stork and various ducks during the winter season. The Minister also encouraged people to visit the site.

passages.text: India’s hopes of reclaiming the title ended in disappointment as they went down 0-3 to France in the semifinals of the Thomas Cup Finals, settling for a bronze medal. The absence of Lakshya Sen proved costly as HS Prannoy joined Ayush Shetty and Kidambi Srikanth in defeat, losing 19-21, 16-21 to world No. 17 Toma Junior Popov, as India failed to win a single game in a completely one-sided contest. India, champions in 2022, had already assured themselves of a medal by reaching the semifinals, adding to their bronze finishes in 1952, 1955 and 1979. With the win, France became only the second European nation to reach the final after Denmark’s maiden title in 2016. Ayush, drafted into the opening singles with Lakshya nursing a swollen right elbow, went down 11-21, 9-21 in 39 minutes to world No. 4 Christo Popov. All eyes were on Srikanth to restore parity, but the former world No. 1 went down fighting 16-21, 18-21 to world No. 10 Alex Lanier in the second singles. The onus was then on Prannoy to keep India alive, and though the 2023 World Championships bronze medallist put up a better fight, he could not get past world No. 17 Popov.

questions.questionText: A student group organises a peaceful event criticising a recently enacted policy. The prohibition appears unjustified because disagreement alone cannot ordinarily justify suppression of expression.
The prohibition is justified because discomfort among influential groups amounts to a threat to public order.

questions.questionText: D, a surgeon performed invasive surgery for appendix removal. The patient’s family wanted laser surgery instead, as it would heal earlier. During the procedure which was conducted with due care and caution, the patient inadvertently developed an infection, which shifted to the intestines. The family blamed the doctor for negligence. Decide whether doctor could be held liable?
options: The doctor is not liable, because he was not negligent, he just chose an alternative medical procedure.
The doctor is not liable, because he was not aware of the potential consequence of invasive surgery.
The doctor is liable because he chose a procedure which amplified the complications.
The doctor is liable because he is responsible for the patient’s infection.

R can claim compensation for negligence only for the actions that were consequent to the negligence of the shop.
R cannot claim compensation because the glass fell on T.
R can claim compensation because he also sustained severe injury.

questions.questionText: G, a shipowner was carrying R’s zebra as a carrier by sea. During a turbulent stormy weather, the zebra turned hostile and behaved violently leading to injuries, despite the best efforts from the crew. Decide whether G could be held liable for negligence?

However, the virus escaped and infected some cattle in the neighbourhood. The infected cattle had to be culled to prevent the infection from spreading further. The owners of the cattle were compensated. Meanwhile a few days later, a cattle auction was scheduled to take place. The cattle auctioneers demanded compensation as well. options: J could be held liable for negligence as the loss to the auctioneers was foreseeable.

passages.text: For more than two decades, India's information technology industry built something genuinely admirable: a world class services engine that became the back office of the global economy. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech, and Tech Mahindra collectively generated hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue, employed millions of engineers, and powered an entire ecosystem of technical education across the country. Then came the AI revolution - and the industry was caught almost entirely unprepared. The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 was not a sudden shock. It was the visible peak of a transformation building since deep learning went mainstream after 2015. But Indian IT firms, locked into low-risk service contracts and investing less than three per cent of revenues in R&D compared to ten to twenty per cent at global technology companies, had neither the incentive nor the institutional culture to see it coming. By the time the alarm was impossible to ignore, the frontier had already been claimed by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a set of well-funded Chinese laboratories. What followed was a period of genuine reckoning. The traditional pyramid model, in which armies of junior engineers churned out standardised code with revenues scaling directly with headcount, began to crack. AI could now perform many of those base layer tasks: routine code generation, testing, data processing, and documentation. At the same time, the growth of over 2,000 Global Capability Centres meant multinationals that once outsourced wholesale were now building substantial in-house teams in India. The existential question became unavoidable: if Indian IT cannot build the AI, and its traditional clients are increasingly building their own teams, what exactly is the industry's role? Four structural failures explain why Indian IT missed the frontier AI race entirely. The first is the services trap. (Source:The Statesman)

passages.text: Feeling depressed about the state of the world? Worried about the future? You're not alone. Pessimism about politics is the new normal among the peoples of the west. Major conflicts in Europe and the Middle East and the harms caused by right-left extremism, stagnating economies, inequality, corruption, terrorism, racism, big tech, mass extinctions and the climate crisis make for shared nightmares. Growing numbers of people simply refuse to personally engage with current events via the news media, finding them too anxiety-inducing (so they probably won't be reading this). In a Reuters Institute survey last year, 40% of respondents in about 50 countries said they sometimes or often avoid the news altogether, a rise of 29% on 2017. Intense negativity characterises European and, to a lesser degree, North American political sentiment. In France, 90% of people questioned by Ipsos believed their country is on the wrong track. In Britain, it was 79%; in Germany, 77%; in the US, 60%. Europeans feel similarly glum about the bigger, global picture, unlike the Chinese, Saudis and Nigerians who are broadly upbeat, according to a GlobeScan survey. Pew Research Center polling in 25 countries last year found that the US, Russia and China are seen, by most but not all, as the biggest international threats. For Turks, for example, Israel is the main menace; for Greeks, it's the Turks. It gets more confusing still. Canada is one of several countries in which majorities regard the US as both the main threat and main ally. Disenchantment with democracy and dissatisfaction with political leaders is a ubiquitous, polarising western phenomenon. Divisions grow entrenched. Keir Starmer, with a 27% approval rating, according to Statista, is struggling to survive. Yet Germany's chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and France's president, Emmanuel Macron, are even less popular, on 19% and 18% respectively. Donald Trump is down to about 38% approval, trailing his nemesis, Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, on 54%. In Russia, Vladimir Putin's historically inflated ratings are now badly punctured. Figures for Xi Jinping are unreliable; in China, freely expressing opinions is dangerous. India is an exception. A majority frankly adores the prime minister, Narendra Modi. (Source: The Gurdian)

passages.text: Recent diplomatic tensions between the United States and Iran have intensified after Iran responded to a U.S.-backed peace proposal with conditions that Washington has described as "unacceptable." The proposal, aimed at ending ongoing conflict and stabilizing the region, includes major demands such as lifting sanctions, a structured 30-day negotiation period, and nuclear-related concessions. However, Iran's counter-response has created fresh disagreements over the terms of peace and the future of regional security. At the centre of the dispute is Iran's demand for complete lifting of U.S. sanctions and unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad. Iran has also insisted on an end to military pressure, including naval restrictions and blockades affecting key trade routes like the Strait of Hormuz. In return, Iran has offered a phased approach to negotiations, suggesting that key issues, including nuclear concerns, could be resolved within a 30-day framework. However, it has refused to dismantle its nuclear infrastructure, which remains a major point of conflict with the U.S. proposal. The United States, on the other hand, has pushed for stricter conditions. These include long-term limits on uranium enrichment, removal of highly enriched uranium stockpiles, and strong verification measures. American officials argue that Iran's proposals do not go far enough to guarantee regional stability or prevent future escalation. Former President Donald Trump, who is closely associated with the negotiations, publicly rejected Iran's response, calling it "totally unacceptable" and warning of possible renewed military action if no agreement is reached. The situation has also impacted global markets and geopolitical stability. Oil prices have fluctuated due to uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy route. Meanwhile, diplomatic mediators, including Pakistan, are attempting to bridge the gap between both sides. In conclusion, the Iran-US negotiations highlight deep mistrust and conflicting expectations. While both sides express willingness to negotiate, differences over sanctions, nuclear policy, and regional control continue to block progress toward a lasting peace agreement. (Source: The telegraph)

According to the Global Burden of Disease study, nearly 197 million Indians - roughly one in seven - live with some form of mental disorder. Depression and anxiety alone affect over 90 million people, yet for most, professional support remains out of reach. For decades, stigma was considered the primary barrier. By 2025, however, the conversation had shifted. Stigma, while still present, was no longer the central obstacle. The more urgent questions had become practical ones: how does care actually function once someone seeks help, and what happens when symptoms escalate? The answer, increasingly, lies in integrated, end-to-end models of care. India's mental health systems were historically built around isolated touchpoints - therapy sessions existed separately from psychiatric care, digital tools operated independently of clinical oversight, and hospitalisation sat at the extreme end of the spectrum, disconnected from what came before and after. Individuals and families were expected to navigate these transitions alone, often during periods of acute vulnerability. Effective systems, experts argue, must allow individuals to move fluidly between levels of support - digital guidance, outpatient care, crisis intervention, and structured inpatient settings - without losing continuity of care. Technology has played a critical role in widening access. The government's Tele-MANAS platform, upgraded in 2025 with a multilingual interface in ten regional languages and an AI-powered chatbot named Asmi, has expanded mental health outreach significantly. Private platforms such as Wysa, Amaha, and Lissun are using AI-driven tools to reach underserved populations. However, a key lesson from 2025 is that access alone is insufficient. Digital tools can open doors, but they cannot substitute for trained professionals or structured clinical care. Looking ahead, India's mental healthcare challenge in 2026 is one of consolidation rather than experimentation. Hospitals, outpatient centres, digital platforms, workplaces, and community networks must function as parts of a coherent whole. Equally important is recognising families not merely as informal caregivers but as active stakeholders in recovery. The opportunity is significant - India has the chance to build a mental healthcare system that is preventative, responsive, and continuous, one that meets people where they are. (Source: National Mental Health Survey of India)

passages.text: Philosophy in the Upaniṣads does not merely consist of abstract claims about the nature of reality, but is also presented as a way of living one's life. In Yājñavalkya's teaching to Janaka, for example, knowledge of atman is associated with a change in one's disposition and behavior. As we have seen, karma is characterized as a natural moral process, with knowledge of the self as a way out of that process. In this respect, a fundamental assumption throughout many teachings of the self is that it is untouched by karma. Yajñavalkya teaches Janaka that knowledge of the self is beyond virtuous (kalyana) and evil (papa)-that, through knowledge of the self one reaches the world of brahman, where the good or bad actions of one's life do not follow. Yajñavalkya explains that in the world of brahman a thief is not a thief, a murderer is not a murderer, an outcaste not an outcaste, a mixed- caste person (paulkasa) is not a mixed-caste person, a renunciate (sramana) is not a renunciate, and an ascetic not an ascetic, that neither the good (punya) nor the evil (papa) follow him. In using these examples Yajñavalkya illustrates the degree to which knowledge of the self is beyond everyday notions of moral behavior. In other words, he seems to be saying that even if one has committed evil deeds, one can still be liberated from karma by means of knowing the self. Yet Yajñavalkya is not suggesting that one can continue to perform 'evil' deeds without suffering karmic retribution. Rather, as he asserts later in his discussion with Janaka: when one is knowledgeable, one necessarily acts morally. Yajñavalkya explains that a man who has proper knowledge becomes calm (santa), restrained (danta), withdrawn (uparata), patient (titiksu), and composed (samaahita). Here Yajñavalkya characterizes knowledge of the self as a change in one's disposition. In other words, one who is a knower of the self becomes a person of good character and-by definition-would not perform an evil action. While Yajñavalkya talks about becoming calm, restrained, withdrawn, patient, and composed, these dispositions are not presented as virtues to cultivate for the sake of knowledge, but rather as consequences of knowing atman. Subsequent texts would devote considerable attention to how one should cultivate oneself in order to achieve the highest knowledge. For example, both the eight-fold path of the Buddhist Nikayas and the eight limbs in the Yoga Sutra suggest that one needs to live a moral life in order to achieve true knowledge. In Yajñavalkya's teaching about atman, however, there is more attention paid to the objective of knowing the self than the ethical means of controlling the self. (Source: https://iep.utm.edu/upanisad)

passages.text: International Humanitarian Law (IHL), also referred to as the law of armed conflict or the law of war, consists of rules intended to limit the effects of armed conflict for humanitarian reasons. Rather than determining whether a war itself is lawful, IHL regulates conduct during armed conflict and seeks to balance military necessity with humanitarian considerations. Its primary objectives are to protect persons who are not, or are no longer, participating in hostilities and to restrict methods and means of warfare that cause unnecessary suffering. IHL principally applies during international and non-international armed conflicts. Among its most fundamental principles is the principle of distinction, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Attacks may lawfully be directed only against military objectives. Civilian persons and civilian objects, such as schools, hospitals, and homes, cannot ordinarily be targeted merely because incidental military advantage may arise from their destruction. Closely related is the principle of proportionality, which prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. This principle does not prohibit all civilian casualties; rather, it seeks to prevent disproportionate harm. Even where a legitimate military objective exists, military operations must not impose excessive burdens on civilians. The principle of military necessity permits only those measures necessary to achieve a legitimate military objective and not otherwise prohibited by international law. However, military necessity does not override all humanitarian obligations. Certain weapons and practices remain prohibited because they cause unnecessary suffering or fail to distinguish between military and civilian targets. Thus, military convenience cannot justify every action during war. Another important principle is humanity, which prohibits means and methods of warfare causing superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering. Torture, cruel treatment, collective punishment, and attacks directed primarily to spread terror among civilians are generally prohibited. Persons who are wounded, detained, or otherwise hors de combat (out of combat) are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of nationality or allegiance. The law also recognises the protection of medical personnel and humanitarian workers. Hospitals and medical units generally enjoy special protection because they serve humanitarian functions. However, such protection may cease if these facilities are used, outside their humanitarian purpose, for acts harmful to the enemy, though reasonable warning may be required before protection is withdrawn. Violations of serious IHL obligations may amount to war crimes. However, superior orders do not automatically excuse unlawful conduct. Individuals may bear responsibility where they knowingly participate in grave violations of humanitarian norms.

passages.text: Constitutional democracies ordinarily distribute governmental authority among different institutions to prevent concentration of power in a single body. This arrangement is reflected in the doctrine of separation of powers, under which legislative bodies generally enact laws, the executive implements and administers them, and the judiciary interprets and applies them. The doctrine does not necessarily require a rigid or absolute division of functions. Modern constitutional systems often permit a degree of overlap because complete separation may be impractical. Nevertheless, the central purpose remains to ensure checks and balances so that no organ exercises uncontrolled power. One of the most significant constitutional mechanisms preserving this balance is judicial review. Judicial review refers to the power of courts to examine the validity of legislative enactments and executive actions and determine whether they conform to constitutional requirements. Courts exercising judicial review do not ordinarily assess whether a law is wise, economically beneficial, or politically desirable. Rather, they examine whether constitutional limitations have been violated. Thus, disagreement with legislative policy is distinct from constitutional invalidity. At the same time, courts generally recognise that elected branches possess institutional competence in certain areas involving policy decisions, economic regulation, allocation of resources, and matters requiring specialised expertise. Therefore, judicial restraint is sometimes considered appropriate where constitutional rights are not directly threatened. However, judicial restraint does not imply judicial abdication. Courts may intervene where governmental actions are arbitrary, violate constitutional guarantees, exceed legal authority, or undermine fundamental rights. The doctrine of checks and balances recognises that constitutional organs may possess limited powers to review or influence one another. Such interaction does not necessarily destroy separation of powers. For instance, executive actions may require legislative approval, legislation may be subject to constitutional scrutiny by courts, and certain appointments or actions may involve more than one branch. Constitutional governance therefore involves both separation and controlled interaction. Another important constitutional principle is the rule of law, which requires that governmental power be exercised according to established legal principles rather than personal discretion or arbitrary preference. Under the rule of law, all individuals and institutions, including public authorities, remain accountable to law. Arbitrary exercises of power are inconsistent with constitutional governance because they undermine predictability, equality, and fairness. Constitutional adjudication also frequently involves balancing majoritarian decision-making and constitutional rights. Democratic institutions ordinarily function according to majority preference. However, constitutional systems recognise that majoritarian support alone cannot justify actions violating fundamental rights. Constitutional guarantees often exist precisely to protect individuals and minority groups from excessive exercises of governmental power.

passages.text: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. It ordinarily involves three parties: the principal debtor, who is primarily liable for the debt or obligation; the creditor, to whom the obligation is owed; and the surety, who undertakes to discharge the liability if the principal debtor fails to do so. The liability of the surety is generally co- extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided by the contract. This means that the surety may be called upon to satisfy the same obligation that the principal debtor was bound to perform. Unlike ordinary contracts, consideration in a contract of guarantee may consist of any act, promise, or benefit done for the benefit of the principal debtor. It is not necessary that the surety receive direct consideration personally. However, a valid guarantee requires free consent, and if consent is obtained through misrepresentation or concealment of material facts, the guarantee may become invalid. For instance, if the creditor deliberately suppresses information regarding the financial condition or conduct of the principal debtor and such information would have influenced the surety's decision, the guarantee may be affected. Guarantees may be specific or continuing. A specific guarantee applies to a single transaction or obligation and comes to an end once that transaction is completed. A continuing guarantee, however, extends to a series of transactions and remains operative until revoked or otherwise terminated according to law. A continuing guarantee may be revoked by the surety concerning future transactions through notice to the creditor. However, such revocation does not affect transactions that have already occurred before the notice was given. Further, the death of a surety ordinarily operates as revocation of a continuing guarantee with respect to future transactions, unless there exists a contract providing otherwise. The law also recognises certain circumstances under which the surety may be discharged from liability. A surety may be discharged if the creditor and principal debtor enter into a contract varying the terms of the original agreement without the surety's consent, where the creditor releases the principal debtor, or where the creditor acts in a manner impairing the surety's eventual remedies against the principal debtor. Such discharge may occur because the surety agreed to guarantee only a specific obligation and should not be subjected to materially altered risks without consent. After satisfying the debt, the surety acquires certain rights against the principal debtor. This principle, often referred to as subrogation, permits the surety to step into the shoes of the creditor and exercise the rights that the creditor could have exercised against the principal debtor. The surety may also claim indemnification from the principal debtor for amounts rightfully paid under the guarantee.

passages.text: The law of tort recognises that a person may not always be held liable for damage merely because harm has occurred. Certain circumstances may excuse liability where the defendant demonstrates that the event occurred despite the exercise of reasonable care and caution. Two closely related yet distinct concepts in this regard are inevitable accident and Act of God (Vis Major). Although both may relieve a defendant from liability, they differ in their origin and legal requirements. An inevitable accident refers to an occurrence which could not have been prevented despite the exercise of reasonable care, caution, and skill by the defendant. The central inquiry is not whether the event caused damage, but whether a reasonable and prudent person exercising ordinary care could have avoided it. The event may arise from human conduct, mechanical failure, or unforeseen circumstances. However, the defendant cannot rely upon inevitable accident where negligence, omission, or lack of proper precautions contributed to the occurrence. Thus, a person who fails to inspect equipment, ignores warning signs, or neglects ordinary safety measures cannot later claim that the accident was inevitable. An Act of God, on the other hand, is a natural event arising exclusively from forces of nature that are so extraordinary and unforeseeable that no amount of human foresight or reasonable care could prevent the resulting damage. Examples may include unprecedented floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or violent natural disturbances. The natural event must operate independently of human intervention and must be so unusual that it could not reasonably have been anticipated. Ordinary seasonal rainfall, predictable weather conditions, or recurring natural events generally do not qualify merely because they cause harm. The distinction between these principles becomes important where natural events and human conduct combine. If a natural event merely contributes to the damage but human negligence substantially contributes to the loss, liability may still arise. Conversely, where the defendant exercised reasonable care and the damage was solely attributable to an extraordinary natural force, the defence of Act of God may succeed. The burden generally lies upon the defendant to establish facts supporting these defences. Further, where a defendant voluntarily undertakes a hazardous activity or introduces potentially dangerous things into their control, courts may closely examine whether reasonable precautions proportionate to the risk were adopted.

passages.text: Criminal liability generally arises where an individual directly commits an offence. However, the law also recognises that a person may be held responsible even without personally carrying out the prohibited act. This principle is reflected in the law relating to abetment, which seeks to punish conduct encouraging, facilitating, or assisting the commission of an offence. The rationale is that a person who deliberately contributes to the commission of an offence may be as blameworthy as the person physically committing it. Abetment may arise in three principal ways: instigation, conspiracy, and intentional aiding. Though these concepts may overlap in certain situations, they are distinct in their legal requirements. Instigation refers to actively provoking, urging, inciting, encouraging, or stimulating another person to commit an act. Such encouragement may be express or implied and may occur through words, conduct, written communication, or even deliberate omission in certain circumstances. However, mere casual remarks, expressions of anger, or statements lacking intention to provoke commission of an offence may not amount to instigation. The focus lies upon whether the accused intended to influence or encourage another person toward committing the act. Abetment by conspiracy occurs where two or more persons agree to commit an unlawful act or agree to commit a lawful act through unlawful means, and some act or illegal omission takes place in furtherance of that agreement. Mere knowledge of an unlawful plan or passive association with conspirators does not by itself constitute conspiracy. There must ordinarily exist a meeting of minds and some step taken toward execution of the common design. Abetment by intentional aiding occurs where a person intentionally facilitates commission of an offence through acts or omissions. Aid may take various forms, including providing tools, information, transport, shelter, or any other assistance that substantially contributes to the offence. Mere presence at the scene of occurrence does not necessarily amount to aiding unless accompanied by conduct intended to facilitate commission of the offence. A person may be liable for abetment even if the principal offence ultimately differs in manner from what was originally intended, provided the consequences are a probable result of the conduct encouraged or assisted. However, where the principal offender acts independently and outside the scope of what was instigated or facilitated, liability for abetment may not arise.
